records.literal_gloss: And came [the] word of Yahweh to Jonah a second [time], saying:

en.L: And the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came to Jonah a second time, saying:
en.B: The word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} came to Jonah a second time:
en.R: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} gave Jonah this message a second time:

pt.L: E a palavra {{divine_name:do SENHOR|de Javé}} veio a Jonas pela segunda vez, dizendo:
pt.B: A palavra {{divine_name:do SENHOR|de Javé}} veio a Jonas pela segunda vez:
pt.R: {{divine_name:O SENHOR|Javé}} deu esta mensagem a Jonas pela segunda vez:

decisions.choice: a second time: the story begins again as in 1:1
decisions.reason: The words repeat 1:1, with "a second time" added. The LORD gives his runaway prophet the same task again. Nothing is said of a rebuke; the commission is simply renewed.

decisions.choice: the same wording as 1:1 at each level
decisions.reason: Each level repeats its own wording of 1:1, so the reader can see that the story starts over.

source.text: ק֛וּם לֵ֥ךְ אֶל־נִֽינְוֵ֖ה הָעִ֣יר הַגְּדוֹלָ֑ה וִּקְרָ֤אאֵלֶ֨יהָ֙ אֶת־הַקְּרִיאָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר אָנֹכִ֖י דֹּבֵ֥ר אֵלֶֽיךָ׃

records.literal_gloss: Arise, go to Nineveh, the great city, and call out to it the proclamation that I [am] speaking to you.

en.L: "Arise, go to Nineveh, the great city, and call out to it the proclamation that I am speaking to you."
en.B: "Get up, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out to it the message that I am giving you."
en.R: "Get up and go to the great city of Nineveh. Announce to its people the message I give you."

pt.L: "Levanta-te, vai a Nínive, a grande cidade, e clama a ela a proclamação que eu te falo."
pt.B: "Levanta-te, vai a Nínive, aquela grande cidade, e clama a ela a mensagem que eu te dou."
pt.R: "Levanta-te e vai à grande cidade de Nínive. Anuncia ao povo dela a mensagem que eu te dou."

decisions.choice: call out to it the proclamation I am speaking to you: Jonah is to say only what God gives him
decisions.reason: In 1:2 the LORD said "call out against it"; here it is "call out to it", and the content is left open: "the proclamation that I am speaking to you". The word for proclamation is used only here in the Bible. The prophet's task is to pass on God's message, whatever it is.

decisions.choice: the same wording as 1:2 for "Arise, go to Nineveh, the great city"; proclamation (L); message (B, R)
decisions.reason: Each level keeps its wording of 1:2 for the repeated words, so that the repeated command can be heard. Readable says "its people" for "it".

source.text: וַיָּ֣קָם יוֹנָ֗ה וַיֵּ֛לֶךְ אֶל־נִֽינְוֶ֖הכִּדְבַ֣ר יְהוָ֑ה וְנִֽינְוֵ֗ה הָיְתָ֤ה עִיר־גְּדוֹלָה֙ לֵֽאלֹהִ֔ים מַהֲלַ֖ךְ שְׁלֹ֥שֶׁת יָמִֽים׃

records.literal_gloss: And arose Jonah and went to Nineveh according to [the] word of Yahweh. And Nineveh was a city great to God, a walk of three days.

en.L: And Jonah arose and went to Nineveh, according to the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. Now Nineveh was a great city to God, a three days' walk.
en.B: So Jonah got up and went to Nineveh, as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} had told him. Now Nineveh was an exceedingly great city, a three days' walk across.
en.R: This time Jonah obeyed {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. He got up and went to Nineveh. Nineveh was a very great city. It took a three days' walk to go across it.

pt.L: E Jonas se levantou e foi a Nínive, segundo a palavra {{divine_name:do SENHOR|de Javé}}. Ora, Nínive era uma cidade grande para Deus, uma caminhada de três dias.
pt.B: Então Jonas se levantou e foi a Nínive, como {{divine_name:o SENHOR|Javé}} lhe tinha dito. Ora, Nínive era uma cidade extremamente grande; eram três dias de caminhada para atravessá-la.
pt.R: Desta vez Jonas obedeceu {{divine_name:ao SENHOR|a Javé}}. Ele se levantou e foi a Nínive. Nínive era uma cidade muito grande. Eram precisos três dias de caminhada para atravessá-la.

decisions.choice: a great city to God: an exceedingly great city
alternatives: a city great even in God's sight
decisions.reason: Hebrew can use the word for God to make something superlative: "mountains of God" are mighty mountains (Psalm 36:7), and "a great camp, like the camp of God" is a vast one (1 Chronicles 12:23). So "great to God" means very great indeed. The wording may also hint at what the end of the book says outright: the city matters to God (4:11).

decisions.choice: a three days' walk: the size of the city
alternatives: the time needed to cross the city
the time needed to go through all its streets
the size of the whole district around the city
decisions.reason: The phrase gives the city's size in days of walking. Its exact sense is not clear: the time to cross it, to visit all of it, or to cover the whole district of greater Nineveh with its towns (Genesis 10:11-12 lists Nineveh with nearby cities as "the great city"). The walls of Nineveh itself, as later excavated, ran about 7 1/2 miles around. The story's point is that the city was huge, too big to be reached in a day.

decisions.choice: according to the word of the LORD: this time Jonah obeys
decisions.reason: In 1:3 Jonah "arose to flee"; here he "arose and went ... according to the word of the LORD". The repeated "arose" marks the difference.

decisions.choice: a great city to God (L); an exceedingly great city (B); a very great city (R); a three days' walk (all levels)
decisions.reason: As set for Jonah, Literal keeps "a great city to God" and Balanced says "an exceedingly great city" (m1); Readable says "very great". "Three days' walk" stays at every level. Balanced and Readable add "across" to make the phrase read as a measure of size. Readable adds "This time Jonah obeyed" for "according to the word of the LORD", which is what the phrase means after chapter 1 (m3).

source.text: וַיָּ֤חֶל יוֹנָה֙ לָב֣וֹא בָעִ֔יר מַהֲלַ֖ךְ י֣וֹם אֶחָ֑ד וַיִּקְרָא֙ וַיֹּאמַ֔ר ע֚וֹד אַרְבָּעִ֣ים י֔וֹם וְנִֽינְוֵ֖ה נֶהְפָּֽכֶת׃

records.literal_gloss: And began Jonah to go into the city, a walk of one day, and he called out and said, Yet forty days, and Nineveh [will be] overturned.

en.L: And Jonah began to go into the city, a walk of one day, and he called out and said, "Yet forty days, and Nineveh [will be] overturned!"
en.B: Jonah began by going a day's walk into the city, and he called out, "Forty more days, and Nineveh will be overthrown!"
en.R: Jonah went into the city and walked for one whole day, calling out, "In forty days Nineveh will be turned upside down!"

pt.L: E Jonas começou a entrar na cidade, uma caminhada de um dia, e clamou e disse: "Ainda quarenta dias, e Nínive [será] subvertida!"
pt.B: Jonas começou a percorrer a cidade e, depois de um dia de caminhada, clamou: "Mais quarenta dias, e Nínive será derrubada!"
pt.R: Jonas entrou na cidade e andou um dia inteiro, anunciando: "Daqui a quarenta dias Nínive vai ser virada de cabeça para baixo!"

decisions.choice: overturned: destroyed, as Sodom was; and also, unknowingly, turned around
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used for the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:21, 25, 29; Deuteronomy 29:22). Jonah means destruction. But the same verb means to turn or change (Exodus 7:17; 1 Samuel 10:9; Psalm 30:12), and in forty days Nineveh is indeed turned: from its evil ways (verse 10). The word holds both outcomes.

decisions.choice: Jonah's message: five words, with no call to repent and no name of God
decisions.reason: In Hebrew the message is only five words: "Yet forty days, and Nineveh overturned." It does not say who will do it or why, and offers no way out. The people of Nineveh respond anyway (verse 5).

decisions.choice: forty days: a set time of testing and waiting
decisions.reason: Forty days is a common period in the Bible: the flood rains (Genesis 7:4), Moses on the mountain (Exodus 24:18), Elijah's journey to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8). It gave the city time.

decisions.choice: a walk of one day: on the first day of his walk through the city
decisions.reason: Jonah had gone one day's walk into the city of verse 3's three days when he began to call out. The text does not say whether he kept on after that.

decisions.choice: overturned (L); overthrown (B); turned upside down (R)
decisions.reason: Each level chooses an English verb that can carry both senses of the Hebrew (m1): ruin, and a complete change. Readable's "turned upside down" does so in everyday words.

decisions.choice: quarenta dias; subvertida (L); derrubada (B); virada de cabeça para baixo (R)
decisions.reason: Each level chooses a verb that can carry both senses of the Hebrew (m1), ruin and a complete change, as the English does: "subverter", the old word for the overthrow of Sodom, also means to turn upside down; a "derrubada" can be the fall of a city or of a way of ruling; Readable says it in everyday words. "Destruída" would keep only Jonah's meaning. "Quarenta dias" is written in words, as numbers are in running text.

source.text: וַֽיַּאֲמִ֛ינוּ אַנְשֵׁ֥י נִֽינְוֵ֖ה בֵּֽאלֹהִ֑ים וַיִּקְרְאוּ־צוֹם֙ וַיִּלְבְּשׁ֣וּ שַׂקִּ֔ים מִגְּדוֹלָ֖ם וְעַד־קְטַנָּֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And believed [the] men of Nineveh in God, and they proclaimed a fast, and they put on sackcloth, from their great to their small.

en.L: And {{gender:the people|the men}} of Nineveh believed in God, and they called a fast and clothed themselves [in] sackcloth, from their greatest even to their least.
en.B: The people of Nineveh believed God. They called for a fast and dressed in sackcloth, from the greatest to the least of them.
en.R: The people of Nineveh believed God's message. They decided to go without food, and they all put on rough sackcloth. Everyone did this, from the most important people to the least important.

pt.L: E {{gender:as pessoas|os homens}} de Nínive creram em Deus, e convocaram um jejum e se vestiram [de] pano de saco, desde o maior deles até o menor deles.
pt.B: O povo de Nínive creu em Deus. Convocaram um jejum e se vestiram de pano de saco, do maior ao menor deles.
pt.R: O povo de Nínive acreditou na mensagem de Deus. Eles decidiram ficar sem comer, e todos vestiram pano de saco grosseiro. Todos fizeram isso, dos mais importantes aos menos importantes.

decisions.choice: the people of Nineveh believed God: they took his warning as true and acted on it
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used of Abraham, who "believed the LORD" (Genesis 15:6). The people trust that the warning comes from God and turn to him. The narrator calls him "God" throughout the story of Nineveh, not by the name the LORD, which Israel knew.

decisions.choice: a fast and sackcloth: signs of grief and repentance
decisions.reason: To go without food and to wear sackcloth, a coarse cloth of goat or camel hair, were signs of mourning and of humbling oneself before God (1 Kings 21:27; Joel 1:13-14). The whole city, high and low, took part.

decisions.choice: Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching: as Matthew 12:41
decisions.reason: Jesus says that the people of Nineveh will rise at the judgment and condemn his generation, "because they repented at the preaching of Jonah" (Matthew 12:41; Luke 11:32).

decisions.choice: believed in God (L); believed God (B); believed God's message (R); go without food (R); rough sackcloth (R)
decisions.reason: Readable makes plain that the people believed what God said through Jonah, explains a fast as going without food, and adds "rough" to show what sackcloth was. "The men of Nineveh" means all its people, so Literal has a gender setting, as Matthew 12:41 does.

decisions.choice: as pessoas de Nínive, under the gender setting (L); pano de saco
decisions.reason: Literal puts "the men of Nineveh" under the gender setting, as the Portuguese of Matthew 12:41 does ("Homens de Nínive"), since the whole city is meant. Sackcloth is "pano de saco", as elsewhere in the prophets in Portuguese.

source.text: וַיִּגַּ֤ע הַדָּבָר֙ אֶל־מֶ֣לֶךנִֽינְוֵ֔ה וַיָּ֨קָם֙ מִכִּסְא֔וֹ וַיַּעֲבֵ֥ר אַדַּרְתּ֖וֹ מֵֽעָלָ֑יו וַיְכַ֣ס שַׂ֔ק וַיֵּ֖שֶׁב עַל־הָאֵֽפֶר׃

records.literal_gloss: And reached the word to [the] king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne and took off his robe from on him, and covered [himself with] sackcloth, and sat on the ashes.

en.L: And the word reached the king of Nineveh, and he rose up from his throne, and removed his robe from himself, and covered himself [with] sackcloth, and sat on the ashes.
en.B: When the news reached the king of Nineveh, he rose from his throne, laid aside his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth and sat down in the ashes.
en.R: When the king of Nineveh heard about this, he got up from his throne. He took off his royal robes and put on sackcloth. Then he sat down in the ashes.

pt.L: E a palavra chegou ao rei de Nínive, e ele se levantou do seu trono, e tirou de si o seu manto, e se cobriu [de] pano de saco, e se sentou sobre a cinza.
pt.B: Quando a notícia chegou ao rei de Nínive, ele se levantou do trono, tirou o seu manto real, se cobriu de pano de saco e se sentou na cinza.
pt.R: Quando o rei de Nínive ficou sabendo disso, ele se levantou do trono. Tirou as suas roupas de rei e vestiu pano de saco. Depois se sentou na cinza.

decisions.choice: the word: the news of Jonah's message and of the people's response
decisions.reason: The word can mean Jonah's proclamation or the report of what was happening in the city. Either way, the king hears it after the people have already begun to fast; the movement starts among the people and reaches the throne.

decisions.choice: the king of Nineveh: the king is not named
decisions.reason: Elsewhere in the Bible the Assyrian ruler is called "the king of Assyria". This book names him by his city, as it is the city that matters in the story, and gives no name or date.

decisions.choice: rose from his throne, took off his robe, sat in the ashes: the king humbles himself
decisions.reason: Each act reverses his royal state: from the throne to the ashes, from the royal robe to sackcloth. Sitting in ashes or dust was a sign of deep grief and repentance (Job 2:8; 42:6; Isaiah 58:5).

decisions.choice: royal robe (B); royal robes (R)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word means a fine cloak, here the king's. Balanced and Readable add "royal" to make that plain.

source.text: וַיַּזְעֵ֗ק וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ בְּנִֽינְוֵ֔ה מִטַּ֧עַם הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ וּגְדֹלָ֖יו לֵאמֹ֑ר הָאָדָ֨ם וְהַבְּהֵמָ֜ה הַבָּקָ֣ר וְהַצֹּ֗אן אַֽל־יִטְעֲמוּ֙ מְא֔וּמָה אַ֨ל־יִרְע֔וּ וּמַ֖יִם אַל־יִשְׁתּֽוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And he had it proclaimed and said in Nineveh, by decree of the king and his great ones, saying: The man and the beast, the herd and the flock, let them not taste anything; let them not graze, and water let them not drink.

en.L: And he had [it] proclaimed, and he said in Nineveh, by the decree of the king and his nobles, saying: "{{gender:Humans|Man}} and beast, herd and flock, let them not taste anything; let them not graze, and let them not drink water.
en.B: Then he had a proclamation made in Nineveh: "By order of the king and his nobles: Let no person or animal, herd or flock, taste anything at all. They must not graze, and they must not drink water.
en.R: Then he sent out this order to everyone in Nineveh: "This is a command from the king and his nobles: No person or animal may eat anything. Do not let the cattle, sheep or goats graze. Nobody, not even the animals, may drink any water.

pt.L: E ele fez proclamar e disse em Nínive, por decreto do rei e dos seus nobres, dizendo: "{{gender:O ser humano|O homem}} e o animal, o gado e o rebanho, não provem coisa alguma; não pastem, e não bebam água.
pt.B: Então ele mandou fazer uma proclamação em Nínive: "Por ordem do rei e dos seus nobres: Nenhuma pessoa ou animal, gado ou rebanho, prove coisa alguma. Não pastem, nem bebam água.
pt.R: Então ele mandou esta ordem a todos em Nínive: "Esta é uma ordem do rei e dos seus nobres: Ninguém, nem pessoa nem animal, pode comer nada. Não deixem o gado, as ovelhas e as cabras pastar. Ninguém, nem mesmo os animais, pode beber água.

decisions.choice: the decree of the king and his nobles: an official proclamation
decisions.reason: The word for decree is a term for the order of a ruler, used of royal commands in Ezra and Daniel. The king acts with his nobles, his great men, so that the order carries the full weight of the state.

decisions.choice: people and animals: the whole city, its animals included, is to fast
decisions.reason: Including the animals makes the fast total: no living thing in the city is to eat or drink. The animals also share in the sackcloth (verse 8). God's last words in the book mention the animals of Nineveh (4:11).

decisions.choice: Humans and beast (L); person or animal (B, R); cattle, sheep or goats (R)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word for human beings is inclusive here, set against the animals; Literal gives it a gender setting, and Balanced and Readable say "person". Readable spells out "herd and flock" as cattle, sheep and goats, and makes clear that the animals too are not to drink. The decree runs to the end of verse 9.

source.text: וְיִתְכַּסּ֣וּ שַׂקִּ֗ים הָֽאָדָם֙ וְהַבְּהֵמָ֔ה וְיִקְרְא֥וּ אֶל־אֱלֹהִ֖ים בְּחָזְקָ֑ה וְיָשֻׁ֗בוּ אִ֚ישׁ מִדַּרְכּ֣וֹ הָֽרָעָ֔ה וּמִן־הֶחָמָ֖ס אֲשֶׁ֥ר בְּכַפֵּיהֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And let them cover themselves [with] sackcloth, the man and the beast, and let them call to God with strength, and let them turn, each from his evil way and from the violence that [is] in their palms.

en.L: And let them cover themselves [with] sackcloth, {{gender:humans|man}} and beast, and let them call to God with strength, and let them turn, each from {{gender:their|his}} evil way and from the violence that [is] in their palms.
en.B: People and animals alike must be covered with sackcloth. Let them call out to God with all their might, and let each one turn from {{gender:their|his}} evil ways and from the violence they do.
en.R: Everyone, people and animals, must wear sackcloth. Everyone must pray to God with all their strength. They must all stop doing evil things and stop hurting others.

pt.L: E cubram-se [de] pano de saco, {{gender:o ser humano|o homem}} e o animal, e clamem a Deus com força, e voltem-se, cada um do seu mau caminho e da violência que [está] nas suas palmas.
pt.B: Pessoas e animais, todos devem se cobrir de pano de saco. Clamem a Deus com toda a força, e cada um se afaste dos seus maus caminhos e da violência que pratica.
pt.R: Todos, pessoas e animais, devem vestir pano de saco. Todos devem orar a Deus com toda a força. Todos devem parar de fazer o mal e parar de machucar os outros.

decisions.choice: the violence that is in their palms: the wrong they do with their own hands
decisions.reason: Violence "in the hands" is wrong a person does and holds on to, whether cruelty or what was gained by it (Job 16:17; Isaiah 59:6). The king names the city's sin plainly. Assyria was known for the violence of its conquests (Nahum 3:1).

decisions.choice: turn from his evil way: repent, change one's whole way of life
decisions.reason: To "turn" is the Bible's word for repentance. "Evil" is the word used of Nineveh in 1:2. The king asks for more than fasting; he asks for a change of life (Jeremiah 18:11; 25:5).

decisions.choice: with strength (L); with all their might (B); with all their strength (R); the violence they do (B); stop hurting others (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what calling "with strength" means. They also turn "the violence in their palms" into the violence people do (m1). "Each" means every person in the city, so "his" takes a gender setting at Literal and Balanced; Readable says "they".

decisions.choice: cada um do seu mau caminho, with no gender setting on "seu"
decisions.reason: The English puts "his" under the gender setting after "each"; Portuguese "seu" is the same word for his and her, and "cada um" already means every person, so there is no second wording to offer. "O ser humano" keeps the setting where the English has "humans".

source.text: מִֽי־יוֹדֵ֣עַ יָשׁ֔וּב וְנִחַ֖ם הָאֱלֹהִ֑ים וְשָׁ֛ב מֵחֲר֥וֹן אַפּ֖וֹ וְלֹ֥א נֹאבֵֽד׃

records.literal_gloss: Who knows? He may turn and relent, the God, and turn from [the] burning of his anger, and we will not perish.

en.L: Who knows? God may turn and relent, and turn from the burning of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} anger, and we will not perish."
en.B: Who knows? God may yet turn and change {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mind; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} may turn back from {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} fierce anger, and we will not perish."
en.R: Who knows? God may change {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mind and stop being angry with us. Then we will not die."

pt.L: Quem sabe? Deus pode se voltar e desistir, e se desviar do ardor da {{deity_pronoun:sua|Sua}} ira, e não pereceremos."
pt.B: Quem sabe? Talvez Deus ainda se volte e desista; talvez {{deity_pronoun:ele|Ele}} se afaste da {{deity_pronoun:sua|Sua}} ira ardente, e não pereceremos."
pt.R: Quem sabe? Talvez Deus mude de ideia e pare de ficar irado conosco. Então não vamos morrer."

decisions.choice: relent: change his mind, turn from a course he has announced
decisions.reason: The verb is used of God turning from a punishment he has threatened when people turn from their sin (Exodus 32:12, 14; Jeremiah 18:8; Joel 2:13-14). It does not mean that God has made a mistake; it means that he responds to people. The same verb is used in verse 10 and in Jonah's complaint (4:2).

decisions.choice: Who knows? God may turn and relent: the same hope as Joel 2:14
decisions.reason: Joel 2:14 says "Who knows? He may turn and relent", and Moses prays "Turn from your burning anger, and relent" (Exodus 32:12). The king of Nineveh, who does not know Israel's God, hopes in the same words. He claims nothing; he can only hope.

decisions.choice: and we will not perish: the captain's words in 1:6
decisions.reason: The ship's captain said "Perhaps the god will give a thought to us, and we will not perish". The pagan king and the pagan captain hope for the same mercy.

decisions.choice: relent (L); change his mind (B, R); the burning of his anger (L); fierce anger (B); perish (L, B); die (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "change his mind" for "relent". Literal and Balanced keep "perish", as in 1:6 (m3). The double quotation mark closes the king's decree.

decisions.choice: desistir (L, B); mudar de ideia (R); não pereceremos (L, B)
decisions.reason: For the whole book: God relenting is "desistir" at Literal and Balanced and "mudar de ideia" at Readable, as Jeremiah 4:28 and 18:8 and Joel 2:14 set it in Portuguese; "arrepender-se" would suggest sorrow for a wrong done (m1). The king's "Quem sabe? Talvez ... se volte e desista" keeps the words of Joel 2:14 (m2), and "não pereceremos" repeats the captain's words in 1:6 (m3).

source.text: וַיַּ֤רְא הָֽאֱלֹהִים֙ אֶֽת־מַ֣עֲשֵׂיהֶ֔ם כִּי־שָׁ֖בוּ מִדַּרְכָּ֣ם הָרָעָ֑ה וַיִּנָּ֣חֶם הָאֱלֹהִ֗ים עַל־הָרָעָ֛ה אֲשֶׁר־דִּבֶּ֥ר לַעֲשׂוֹת־לָהֶ֖ם וְלֹ֥א עָשָֽׂה׃

records.literal_gloss: And saw the God their deeds, that they turned from their evil way; and relented the God concerning the evil which he had said to do to them, and he did not do [it].

en.L: And God saw their deeds, that they had turned from their evil way; and God relented concerning the evil that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had said {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} would do to them, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did not do [it].
en.B: When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil ways, God relented of the disaster {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had said {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} would bring on them, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did not do it.
en.R: God saw what they did. He saw that they had stopped doing evil. So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} changed {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mind and did not bring on them the disaster {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had said {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} would bring.

pt.L: E Deus viu as obras deles, que se voltaram do seu mau caminho; e Deus desistiu do mal que {{deity_pronoun:ele|Ele}} tinha dito que lhes faria, e não [o] fez.
pt.B: Quando Deus viu o que fizeram, como se afastaram dos seus maus caminhos, Deus desistiu da desgraça que {{deity_pronoun:ele|Ele}} tinha dito que traria sobre eles, e não a trouxe.
pt.R: Deus viu o que eles fizeram. Viu que tinham parado de fazer o mal. Então {{deity_pronoun:ele|Ele}} mudou de ideia e não trouxe sobre eles a desgraça que tinha dito que traria.

decisions.choice: their evil way ... the evil he had said he would do: one word for their wickedness and for the disaster
decisions.reason: The same word, used throughout the book (see 1:2), names the evil the people did and the evil, that is the disaster, God threatened. When they turned from the one, God turned from the other, as Jeremiah 18:7-8 describes.

decisions.choice: God relented: the threatened judgment was not carried out
decisions.reason: Jonah's message gave no condition, but the story shows that God's warnings call people to turn (Jeremiah 18:7-10). Elsewhere Scripture says that God does not change his mind as a human does (Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29). Both speak of the same God: his purpose stands, and he answers those who turn to him. This is what Jonah complains of in 4:2.

decisions.choice: God saw their deeds: he responded to what they did, not only to their fast
decisions.reason: It was their turning from evil, the change in their lives that the king called for (verse 8), that God saw.

decisions.choice: evil ... evil (L); evil ways ... disaster (B); evil ... disaster (R); relented (L, B); changed his mind (R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "evil" twice so the reader can see the one word (m1). Balanced and Readable say "disaster" for what God threatened. Readable says "changed his mind", as in verse 9.

decisions.choice: mau caminho ... o mal (L); desistiu (L, B); mudou de ideia (R)
decisions.reason: Literal says "mal" for both the people's evil and the harm God threatened (m1), as in 1:2; "desistiu do mal" is the Portuguese of Jeremiah 18:8 at Literal. Portuguese leaves out the repeated subject pronouns where the English writes "he had said he would ... he did not", so fewer deity_pronoun spans are needed.
